meta.title: Understanding Inflation
meta.blurb: Why does a snack cost more than it used to? That's inflation. Learn what causes it and how to keep up.
objectives: See how prices change over time
meta.outcome: By the end, you can explain why saving alone isn't always enough.

modules.title: The basics
modules.summary: Watch the video, then learn the key ideas.
modules.discussionPrompt: What's something you buy that costs more now than a year ago?

blocks.md:
Inflation means prices go up over time. When prices rise, each dollar buys a little less.

**A quick example**
If a snack costs $1.00 this year and $1.03 next year, prices rose 3%. Your dollar didn't change, but it buys less.

**Purchasing power**
That's how much your money can actually buy. Inflation slowly shrinks it.

**Is some inflation normal?**
Yes. A little inflation is expected in a healthy economy. In the US, the Federal Reserve aims for about 2% a year over time.

Problems start when inflation gets high. Then prices climb faster than paychecks.
**Parent tip:** Ask grandparents what a movie ticket or a gallon of milk cost when they were young. It makes inflation real for kids.

The most common measure in the US is the **Consumer Price Index**, or **CPI**.

**How it works**
The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks prices of a "basket" of things people buy. That includes food, rent, gas, clothing, medical care and more.

Each month, they check how much the basket costs. If it costs 3% more than a year ago, inflation is about 3%.

**Your inflation may be different**
The basket is an average. If you spend a lot on something rising fast, like rent, your costs may rise faster than the CPI.

**Real vs nominal**
• **Nominal** means the plain number, like a 4% raise
• **Real** means after inflation. With 3% inflation, a 4% raise is about a 1% real raise

blocks.md:
Inflation usually comes from a few big causes.

**Too much demand**
When lots of people want to buy, but there isn't enough to go around, prices rise.

**Higher costs**
When it costs more to make things, like fuel or materials, businesses often raise prices.

**More money in the system**
If money grows faster than the goods to buy, each dollar is worth less.

**What the Federal Reserve does**
To slow inflation, the Fed can raise interest rates. Borrowing gets more expensive, people spend less, and prices cool down. To help a slow economy, it can lower rates.

**Expectations matter too**
If people expect prices to rise, they may buy now and ask for raises. That can push prices up further.

items.title: How to keep up with inflation

blocks.md:
You can't stop inflation, but you can plan for it.

**Don't let cash sit idle**
Money in a 0% account loses buying power. Keep emergency money in a savings account that pays interest.

**Invest for the long term**
For money you won't need for many years, investing has usually grown faster than inflation. It goes up and down along the way.

**Look at inflation-protected options**
• **TIPS:** Treasury bonds that adjust for inflation
• **I bonds:** US savings bonds with a rate tied to inflation, bought at TreasuryDirect.gov

**Grow your earning power**
New skills can lead to raises that beat inflation.

**Update your budget**
Check your budget when prices change, so it stays real.
**Try this:** Use the inflation tool in Module 2. See what $100 will buy in 20 years at 3%.

question.prompt: Which can help savings keep up with inflation over many years?
question.hint: You need growth that beats rising prices.
question.explanation: Over long periods, diversified investing has usually grown faster than inflation, though it can drop in the short term.
